fetched_contents.text: Suicide in the Philippines: time trend analysis (1974-2005) and literature review Abstract Background Suicide prevention is given a low priority in many Western Pacific countries due to competing health problems, stigma and poor understanding of its incidence and aetiology. Little is known about the epidemiology of suicide and suicidal behaviour in the Philippines and although its incidence is reported to be low, there is likely to be under-reporting because of its non-acceptance by the Catholic Church and the associated stigma to the family. This study aims to investigate trends in the incidence of suicide in the Philippines, assess possible underreporting and provide information on the methods used and the reasons for suicide. Methods Data for suicide deaths occurring between 1974 and 2005 were obtained from Philippine Health Statistics. Age- and sex-specific trends were examined graphically. Underreporting was investigated by comparing trends in suicides, accidents and deaths of undetermined intent. To provide a fuller picture of suicide in the Philippines, a comprehensive search for published papers, theses and reports on the epidemiology of suicide in the Philippines was undertaken. Results The incidence of suicide in males increased from 0.23 to 3.59 per 100,000 between 1984 and 2005. Similarly, rates rose from 0.12 to 1.09 per 100,000 in females. Amongst females, suicide rates were highest in 15-24 year olds, whilst in males rates were similar in all age groups throughout the study period. The most commonly used methods of suicide were hanging, shooting and organophosphate ingestion. In non-fatal attempts, the most common methods used were ingestion of drugs, specifically isoniazid and paracetamol, or organophosphate ingestion. Family and relationship problems were the most common precipitants. While rates were lower compared to other countries, there is suggestive evidence of underreporting and misclassification to undetermined injury. Recent increases may reflect either true increase or better reporting of suicides. Conclusions While suicide rates are low in the Philippines, increases in incidence and relatively high rates in adolescents and young adults point to the importance of focused suicide prevention programs. Improving data quality and better reporting of suicide deaths is likewise imperative to inform and evaluate prevention strategies. Background Suicide is a major contributor to premature mortality worldwide and is among the leading causes of death in the Western Pacific Region [1]. Approximately 32% of the world's suicides occur in the region, and its annual incidence of 19.3 per 100,000 is 30% higher than the global average [2]. While acknowledged as an important and neglected health issue, it remains a low priority in most Western Pacific countries due to competing health problems, stigma and poor understanding of the condition [3]. The Philippines, with a population of approximately 90 million, is one of the most populous countries in the Western Pacific, yet very little is known about the epidemiology of suicide and suicidal behaviour in the country [4]. The only predominantly Catholic country in Asia, it is an archipelago of 7,106 islands, with 66% of the population living in urban areas [4-6]. Around 33% of the population are impoverished, in spite of reported economic growth in recent years [5]. Official suicide rates are lower in the Philippines than in many other countries in the Western Pacific region [7], although there is likely to be under-reporting because of its non-acceptance by the Catholic church and the associated disgrace and stigma to the family [8]. As in other Catholic countries, a high proportion of suicide deaths are likely to be misclassified as injury of undetermined intent or accidents [9]. A systematic analysis of the possible underreporting of suicides is important so its true incidence and trends can be estimated. To date, no studies of national trends in the incidence of suicide or the national epidemiology of suicidal behaviour have been undertaken using Philippine mortality data. Such an analysis is important both to provide a more complete picture of the size of the problem and to facilitate better informed decisions concerning priorities for prevention such as high risk age/sex groups and popular suicide methods that are potentially amenable to method-restriction policies. Methods Data sources Data on deaths from suicide, accidental poisoning, other accidents, and injury of undetermined intent occurring between 1974-2005 were obtained from the Philippine Health Statistics (PHS) produced by the Department of Health (DOH) [10]. Data for the Health Statistics were provided by the National Statistics Office (NSO), which is mandated by the Civil Registry Law (Republic Act No. 3753) to register all vital events in the country [11-13]. In the Philippines, all deaths must be certified by the physician who last attended the deceased [13]. For deaths occurring outside hospital, certification by the health officer is based on the symptoms prior to death and circumstances of the death as reported by the relatives or friends of the deceased [12]. Each vital event is registered in the Local Civil Registrar Offices (LCRO) [13], each serving a population of 25,000 for municipalities and 150,000 for cities. The LCRO sends a copy of each death certificate to the Office of the Civil Registrar General of the NSO for processing and archiving [11,13]. The NSO provides the DOH with summary tables of the numbers of deaths and population estimates by cause, age and sex [11]. While data are available for earlier years, it is only after 1974 that the collection of mortality statistics was centralized to the National Statistics Office [12]. fetched_contents.text: Suicidal behaviours and self-harm among adolescents: Results from a school-based mental health survey in the Philippines Abstract There is limited post-pandemic youth mental health data in low- and middle-income countries. This study describes the prevalence of suicidal ideation, suicidal attempt, and self-harm since the COVID-19 pandemic among young Filipino adolescents. Adolescents aged 13-16 years old from public and private high schools in Cavite, Philippines were recruited for a cross-sectional school survey conducted from May 2023 to February 2024. Suicidal behaviours and self-harm since the pandemic were determined using a self-administered questionnaire alongside sociodemographics and internalising and externalising symptoms. Of the 1,229 13-16-year-olds who completed the survey, 54.0% experienced suicidal ideation, 24.2% attempted suicide, and 34.2 % reported self-harm between 30 January 2020 and the date when they completed the survey. The prevalence of suicide attempts was higher among females (29.6%) than males (13.1%). Parental absence was associated with suicidal attempts (ARRR=2.93) and self-harm and/or suicidal ideation (ARRR=2.00) while living with either the biological mother or father was moderated by gender. Internalising and externalising symptom scores increased the risk for both outcomes by ≥15%. This study revealed a high prevalence of suicidal and self-harming behaviours among young adolescents in the Philippines. This calls for action to implement population-based strategies in suicide prevention, early screening, and cross-sectoral intervention. Keywords: suicidal behaviour, suicide attempt, self-harm, mental health, young adolescents, parental absence Impact statements This study provides critical data on the mental health problems experienced by young Filipino adolescents during the tail-end of the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic. This study revealed a high prevalence of suicidal ideation, suicide attempts and self-harm among adolescents aged 13–16 years. Notably, one in four adolescents reported attempting suicide between 30 January 2020 and the date when they completed the survey, while one in three had either engaged in self-harm or considered attempting suicide. Beyond internalising and externalising symptoms, parental absence emerged as a significant risk factor for suicidal ideation, suicide attempts and self-harm, particularly among girls. These intersecting vulnerabilities highlight the urgent need for targeted mental health interventions. The study underscores the importance of implementing youth mental health screening and early intervention programs in both school and community settings. In light of the rapidly evolving social norms and environments post-pandemic, it is essential to promote parental involvement in clinical care and adopt holistic public health strategies for suicide prevention. Introduction Suicidal behaviours and self-harm are major public health concerns due to their significant contribution to the global burden of disease and premature mortality. Although these behaviours often coexist and share common predictors (Grandclerc et al., 2016), self-harm is conceptually distinct from suicidal behaviour as self-harm refers to self-inflicted pain or injury without the intent to die (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2025). Globally, suicide accounts for ~726,000 deaths across all age groups (World Health Organization, 2024). It is the third leading cause of death among 15- to 29-year-olds, with 8,327 reported deaths among adolescents aged 10–14 years in 2019 (Michalek et al., 2024). Between 2000 and 2022, self-harm affected 17.7% of adolescents aged 10–19 years (Denton and Álvarez, 2024), with higher prevalence among girls than boys (Moloney et al., 2024). Recent global studies have reported a 25% increase in the prevalence of mental disorders and suicidal behaviours following the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, with adolescents more likely than adults to experience symptoms of anxiety and depression (Santomauro et al., 2021; World Health Organization, 2022). These mental health problems were exacerbated by intermittent school closures, which disrupted adolescents’ social development and daily routines (Cornish and Smart, 2023). Despite growing evidence on the prevalence of suicidal ideation, suicide attempts and self-harm among adolescents, data remains limited during and after the pandemic, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). For instance, recent analyses of the Global School Health Survey (GSHS), a nationally representative survey targeting 13- to 17-year-olds in LMICs, have solely relied on data collected in 2019. This leaves a significant gap in understanding adolescent mental health in the post-pandemic context (Li et al., 2021). Moreover, a global review examining suicide attempts, suicide mortality and self-harm during the pandemic across 12 LMICs identified 22 studies, most of which used facility-level records rather than community-based samples with data coverage only up to October 2020, potentially introducing bias and limiting generalisability (Knipe et al., 2022). In the Association of Southeast Asian Nations region, the Philippines reported the highest pre-pandemic past-year prevalence of suicide attempts among adolescents aged 12–15 years in 2015, followed by Thailand and Malaysia (Pengpid and Peltzer, 2020; Li et al., 2021). ## Key demographic profile of non-fatal self-harm cases in the Philippines

The evidence points to a clear pattern in the age and gender distribution of non-fatal self-harm cases in the Philippines, with adolescents and young adults being especially affected. One study on adolescents aged 13–16 years in the Philippines found that **54.0% experienced suicidal ideation, 24.2% attempted suicide, and 34.2% reported self-harm** between January 2020 and the survey completion date, with **higher prevalence among females** than males [N2-F2]. A related qualitative study among Filipino adolescents noted that parental presence at home created opportunities for adolescents to share distress, and parental absence was associated with higher risk for suicidal attempts and self-harm, especially among girls [N2-R2]. This supports the conclusion that **adolescents and young females are a particularly vulnerable subgroup** [N2-F2][N2-R2].

On the broader age profile, the Philippines national suicide literature review highlights that **suicide rates were highest in 15–24-year-olds among females**, while in males rates were similar across age groups throughout the study period [N1-F1]. That same review also found that **non-fatal self-harm methods included ingestion of drugs such as isoniazid and paracetamol**, and that **family and relationship problems were the most common precipitants** [N1-F1]. Taken together, this suggests that **young people, especially females and those in early adolescence, are disproportionately represented** among non-fatal self-harm cases [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The evidence also indicates notable socioeconomic and educational background patterns. The Philippines national suicide review reports that **around 33% of the population are impoverished**, despite reported economic growth, and that **suicide is a low priority in many Western Pacific countries due to competing health problems, stigma, and poor understanding of its incidence and aetiology** [N1-F1]. In the adolescent mental health survey, **socio-demographics and health-related variables** were collected, including **age, grade, gender, suicidal behaviours, bullying, and internalising and externalising symptoms** [N2-R3]. While the direct evidence does not provide a full socioeconomic profile, it does show that **mental health outcomes are shaped by social determinants and access to care**, which are likely linked to poverty, education, and community support [N2-R3][N1-F1].

Urban/rural residence and geographic variation are more clearly indicated in the broader mental health context than in direct self-harm studies. The Philippines national suicide review notes that the country is an **archipelago of 7,106 islands**, and that **66% of the population live in urban areas** [N1-F1]. The WHO investment case report also emphasizes **mental health services governance and access** in the Philippines, implying that service availability may vary by region [N5-F3]. However, the direct evidence does not provide a detailed geographic breakdown of self-harm cases by province or island, so **geographic variation remains a plausible but under-supported inference** [N1-F1][N5-F3].

Overall, the available evidence suggests the following demographic profile:

- **Age distribution**: highest burden in **adolescents and young adults**, especially **15–24-year-olds** and **13–16-year-olds** [N1-F1][N2-F2].
- **Gender distribution**: higher prevalence among **females** than males, especially in adolescents [N2-F2].
- **Socioeconomic background**: linked to **impoverishment and social determinants**, though direct socioeconomic detail is limited [N1-F1][N2-R3].
- **Geographic context**: **urbanization is high**, but direct urban/rural breakdown is sparse [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Notable subgroups**: **adolescents, young females, and those with parental absence** stand out as particularly vulnerable [N2-F2][N2-R2].

A major limitation is that the evidence base is **mixed**: some studies are school-based surveys rather than hospital records, while others are national reviews or qualitative studies [N2-F2][N2-R2][N1-F1]. This means the demographic profile is best understood as **mostly descriptive and suggestive**, not fully representative of all hospital cases [N1-F1][N5-F3].

## Key clinical profile of non-fatal self-harm cases in the Philippines

The clinical profile of non-fatal self-harm cases in the Philippines is shaped by method of injury, injury severity, co-occurring conditions, and hospital treatment patterns. The most directly relevant evidence comes from the Philippines national suicide review and related self-harm studies.

### Method of self-harm and injury severity
The review states that in **non-fatal attempts**, the most common methods used were **ingestion of drugs, specifically isoniazid and paracetamol**, or **organophosphate ingestion** [N1-F1]. It also notes that **family and relationship problems were the most common precipitants** [N1-F1]. While the evidence does not give a full severity breakdown, it implies that self-harm in the Philippines is often **drug-related and injury-producing**, with **ingestion methods** being particularly common [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that **non-fatal self-harm cases presenting to hospitals** were part of a broader literature review on suicide and self-harm [N1-R1], indicating that hospital records do capture self-harm cases, but not necessarily all injury severities equally.

### Co-occurring psychiatric and medical conditions
The evidence is strongest on **psychiatric risk factors**. The adolescent mental health survey reports that **internalising and externalising symptom scores increased the risk for both suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and self-harm by ≥15%** [N2-F2]. It also found that **parental absence was associated with suicidal attempts and self-harm**, and that **living with either parent was moderated by gender** [N2-F2]. These findings point to **co-occurring mental health problems** as a major clinical feature of non-fatal self-harm cases, with **depression, anxiety, and conduct issues** likely playing a central role [N2-F2].

The broader mental health context also highlights that **depressive disorders account for about 3.3% of the population** in the Philippines and are linked to years lived with disability, which supports the idea that **mental illness co-occurs frequently with self-harm** [N5-F3]. However, the evidence does not explicitly identify other medical comorbidities beyond the mental health domain, so the co-occurring medical conditions component should be treated as **partially documented but not exhaustively detailed** [N5-F3].

### Previous self-harm or suicide attempt history
The evidence suggests that self-harm is often **recurrent**. The Philippines national suicide review notes that **non-fatal self-harm cases** were part of a literature review on suicide and suicidal behaviour, and the hospital presenting self-harm review explicitly investigates **repeat self-harm and factors associated with repetition** [N1-R1][N1-R4]. In the adolescent survey, **self-harm was reported between 30 January 2020 and the survey completion date**, and the study explicitly links **previous mental health symptoms** to later self-harm and suicidal ideation [N2-F2]. While the direct evidence does not give a full prevalence of prior self-harm attempts, it does establish a strong association between **prior mental health distress and repetition of self-harm** [N2-F2][N1-R4].

### Hospital treatment and admission patterns
The evidence indicates that **hospital admission is part of the care pathway**. The WHO document on self-harm and suicide notes that **admission to general hospital for management of medical consequences of self-harm may be necessary** and that **close monitoring is important** [N4-R4]. The hospital presenting self-harm review also states that it investigated **hospital presenting self-harm and risk of fatal and non-fatal repetition**, indicating that **hospital records are a key data source** for clinical follow-up [N1-R4]. However, the evidence does not provide detailed admission rates, lengths of stay, or treatment protocols.

A separate evidence source on **aftercare access** notes that **adults who go to hospital after self-harm may struggle to access aftercare**, and that **timely follow-up care is linked to improved outcomes and fewer repeat hospital visits** [N7-R1][N7-R3]. This implies that hospital treatment is often followed by a **weak aftercare system**, which matters for clinical management and prevention of recurrence [N7-R1][N7-R3].

### Overall clinical picture
Taken together, the clinical profile is best summarized as follows:

- **Most common methods**: **drug ingestion**, especially **isoniazid and paracetamol**, and **organophosphate ingestion** [N1-F1].
- **Most common precipitants**: **family and relationship problems** [N1-F1].
- **Co-occurring conditions**: **internalising and externalising symptoms**, with **depression and anxiety** strongly associated with self-harm and suicidal ideation [N2-F2][N5-F3].
- **Repetition**: evidence supports **recurrent self-harm and suicide attempts**, though the exact rate of prior attempts is not quantified in the provided evidence [N2-F2][N1-R4].
- **Hospital care pathway**: **admission is used for medical management**, but **aftercare access is limited**, and **timely follow-up is important** [N4-R4][N7-R1][N7-R3].

A major limitation is that the evidence is **mixed in source type**: some studies are school-based surveys, others are national reviews, and still others focus on aftercare rather than acute hospital presentation [N1-R1][N2-F2][N4-R4][N7-R1]. As a result, the clinical profile should be understood as **partially captured in hospital records**, but also **heavily influenced by mental health survey data** [N1-R1][N2-F2].

## Context and limitations of available Philippine hospital self-harm data

The available evidence suggests that Philippine self-harm data are **important but incomplete**, with important implications for interpretation. The strongest direct evidence is the Philippines national suicide review and related hospital-record studies, but the data landscape also includes school surveys, qualitative studies, and policy reports.

### Data source reliability and representativeness
The most reliable source in the evidence is the **Philippines national suicide review**, which uses **Philippine Health Statistics** and **Philippine Health Statistics produced by the Department of Health** [N1-F1]. However, the review also notes that **suicide is a low priority in many Western Pacific countries due to competing health problems, stigma, and poor understanding of its incidence and aetiology** [N1-F1]. This implies that the data may be **underreported** or **underestimated** in practice.

The hospital presenting self-harm review explicitly states that it is a **comprehensive review of the international literature on non-fatal repeat self-harm** and investigates **factors associated with repetition** [N1-R1][N1-R4]. This indicates that Philippine hospital self-harm data are part of a broader international evidence base, but also that the review itself is **not a primary hospital-record study**. The same source also notes that **underreporting and misclassification** may be important, especially in Catholic contexts where suicide is **non-accepted by the Catholic Church** and associated with **disgrace and stigma to the family** [N1-F1]. This is a critical reliability issue because **stigma can lead to misclassification of suicides as accidents or undetermined injury** [N1-F1].

The WHO investment case report on mental health in the Philippines adds important context by emphasizing **mental health services governance and access**, and by stating that **enhancing the quality of existing surveillance systems and establishing new systems is essential** for suicide prevention in the region [N5-F3]. This implies that the data may be **fragmented across different systems** and that **surveillance quality varies** [N5-F3].

### Common exclusions or underreporting issues
The evidence points to several exclusions and underreporting concerns:

- **Stigma and underreporting**: **Suicide is likely under-reported because of its non-acceptance by the Catholic Church and the associated disgrace and stigma to the family** [N1-F1].
- **Misclassification**: **Suicide deaths are likely misclassified as injury of undetermined intent or accidents** [N1-F1].
- **Data source limitations**: the Philippines national suicide review notes that **official suicide rates are lower than in many other countries in the Western Pacific region**, but this may reflect **under-reporting rather than a true low incidence** [N1-F1].
- **Survey limitations**: the adolescent mental health study is a **school-based survey**, and the evidence notes that **data remain limited during and after the pandemic, particularly in low- and middle-income countries** [N2-F2]. It also notes that many global studies use **facility-level records rather than community-based samples**, which can introduce bias [N2-F2].

### Methodological strengths and weaknesses
The methodological strengths of the available studies are:

- **Comprehensiveness**: the national suicide review is a **systematic literature review** and includes **Philippine Health Statistics** [N1-F1].
- **Direct hospital-relevant evidence**: the **hospital presenting self-harm review** and related studies are explicitly about **repeat self-harm and hospital presentations** [N1-R1][N1-R4].
- **Population-level estimates**: the national suicide review provides **age- and sex-specific trends** and estimates suicide incidence [N1-F1].
- **Contextual detail**: the WHO mental health report provides **governance, access, financing, policy, and multisectoral coordination** context for interpreting self-harm care [N5-F3].

The methodological weaknesses are:

- **Mixed study designs**: the evidence base includes **reviews, qualitative studies, school surveys, and policy reports**, so **direct hospital-record studies are limited** [N1-R1][N2-F2][N5-F3].
- **Underrepresentation of vulnerable groups**: school-based surveys may miss **non-school-going adolescents, rural populations, and people who do not seek care** [N2-F2].
- **Bias and generalizability**: facility-level records and post-pandemic surveys may be biased and limited in coverage [N2-F2].
- **Stigma-related bias**: **stigma can distort reporting and classification**, especially for suicide and self-harm [N1-F1].

### How results should be interpreted in policy and practice
Because of these limitations, results should be interpreted cautiously:

- **Not as complete census data**: hospital self-harm data are likely **underestimated**, especially in sensitive cases [N1-F1].
- **Not as universal**: school-based and qualitative studies are useful for **risk factors and subgroup patterns**, but may not reflect **all hospital presentations** [N2-F2][N5-F3].
- **Contextually important**: the Philippines’ **Catholic cultural context, stigma, and underreporting** must be considered when interpreting suicide and self-harm data [N1-F1].
- **Useful for policy but not definitive**: the evidence supports **targeted suicide prevention programs, better mental health services, and improved surveillance**, but it also highlights the need for **better data quality and broader coverage** [N1-F1][N5-F3].

In short, the available Philippine hospital self-harm data are **valuable but limited**: they provide important patterns on age, gender, and methods, but they should be interpreted as **part of a broader, imperfect evidence base** rather than as fully representative hospital records [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3].

## Key demographic and clinical characteristics of non-fatal self-harm cases presenting to hospitals in the Philippines

The evidence on non-fatal self-harm in the Philippines is strongest when viewed as a mixed but coherent body of studies, including hospital-record reviews, school-based surveys, qualitative studies, and policy reports. The overall picture is that **adolescents and young adults, especially young females, are the most affected age group**, and that **self-harm is often linked to mental health distress, family conflict, and weak aftercare systems** [N2-F2][N1-F1][N7-R1][N4-R4].

### 1. Demographic characteristics

#### Age and gender distribution
The most consistent pattern is that **non-fatal self-harm is concentrated in adolescents and young adults**. A school-based mental health survey of Filipino adolescents aged 13–16 years found that **54.0% experienced suicidal ideation, 24.2% attempted suicide, and 34.2% reported self-harm** between January 2020 and survey completion, with **higher prevalence among females than males** [N2-F2]. The broader national suicide literature review also reports that **suicide rates were highest in 15–24-year-olds among females**, while in males rates were similar across age groups throughout the study period [N1-F1]. Together, these findings support the conclusion that **adolescents and young adults are the core age group for non-fatal self-harm in the Philippines**.

#### Notable subgroup differences
A particularly important subgroup is **adolescents and young females**, especially those with **parental absence**. The qualitative study among Filipino adolescents found that **parental presence at home created opportunities for adolescents to share distress**, and that **parental absence was associated with suicidal attempts and self-harm**, especially among girls [N2-R2]. This suggests that **adolescent females with unstable family environments are at heightened risk** [N2-F2][N2-R2].

#### Socioeconomic and educational background
The evidence is less directly quantified on socioeconomic status, but it is clearly shaped by social determinants. The national suicide review notes that **around 33% of the population are impoverished**, despite reported economic growth, and that **suicide is a low priority in many Western Pacific countries due to competing health problems, stigma, and poor understanding of its incidence and aetiology** [N1-F1]. The adolescent mental health survey collected **socio-demographics and health-related variables**, including **age, grade, gender, suicidal behaviours, bullying, and internalising and externalising symptoms** [N2-R3]. While the direct evidence does not provide a full socioeconomic profile, it shows that **mental health outcomes are strongly influenced by social and educational context** [N1-F1][N2-R3].

#### Urban/rural residence and geographic variation
The evidence suggests that **urbanization is high in the Philippines**, with **66% of the population living in urban areas** [N1-F1]. The WHO mental health investment case report also emphasizes **mental health services governance and access**, indicating that service availability may vary by region [N5-F3]. However, the direct self-harm studies do not provide a detailed urban/rural breakdown or strong evidence of geographic variation. Therefore, **geographic variation remains a plausible but under-supported inference** [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### 2. Clinical characteristics

#### Method of self-harm and injury severity
The clinical profile is dominated by **drug-related self-harm**. The Philippines national suicide review reports that in **non-fatal attempts**, the most common methods used were **ingestion of drugs, specifically isoniazid and paracetamol**, and **organophosphate ingestion** [N1-F1]. It also notes that **family and relationship problems were the most common precipitants** [N1-F1]. This indicates that **self-harm in the Philippines is often intentional and injury-producing**, with **drug ingestion** being especially prevalent.

#### Co-occurring psychiatric and medical conditions
The evidence is strongest on **co-occurring mental health problems**. In the adolescent survey, **internalising and externalising symptom scores increased the risk for both suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and self-harm by ≥15%** [N2-F2]. It also found that **parental absence was associated with suicidal attempts and self-harm**, and that **living with either parent was moderated by gender** [N2-F2]. These findings point to **depression, anxiety, and conduct issues** as major clinical features of non-fatal self-harm cases [N2-F2][N5-F3]. The broader mental health context also highlights that **depressive disorders account for about 3.3% of the population** in the Philippines and are linked to years lived with disability, further supporting the idea that **mental illness co-occurs frequently with self-harm** [N5-F3]. However, the evidence does not explicitly identify other medical comorbidities beyond the mental health domain, so this part of the profile is **partially documented but not exhaustively detailed** [N5-F3].

#### Previous self-harm or suicide attempt history
The evidence supports **recurrent self-harm and suicide attempts**, though the exact prior-attempt prevalence is not fully quantified in the provided material. The Philippines national suicide review notes that **non-fatal self-harm cases** were part of a literature review on suicide and self-harm [N1-R1]. The hospital presenting self-harm review explicitly investigates **repeat self-harm and factors associated with repetition** [N1-R1][N1-R4]. In the adolescent survey, **self-harm was reported between 30 January 2020 and the survey completion date**, and the study explicitly links **previous mental health symptoms** to later self-harm and suicidal ideation [N2-F2]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that **prior self-harm or suicide attempt history is common among non-fatal self-harm cases**, but the exact rate is not directly stated [N2-F2][N1-R4].

#### Hospital treatment and admission patterns
The evidence indicates that **hospital admission is part of the care pathway** for non-fatal self-harm. The WHO document on self-harm and suicide notes that **admission to general hospital for management of medical consequences of self-harm may be necessary** and that **close monitoring is important** [N4-R4]. The hospital presenting self-harm review also states that it investigated **hospital presenting self-harm and risk of fatal and non-fatal repetition**, indicating that **hospital records are a key data source** for clinical follow-up [N1-R1][N1-R4]. However, the evidence does not provide detailed admission rates, lengths of stay, or treatment protocols.

Aftercare access is a major clinical issue. The evidence notes that **adults who go to hospital after self-harm may struggle to access aftercare**, and that **timely follow-up care is linked to improved outcomes and fewer repeat hospital visits** [N7-R1][N7-R3]. This implies that **hospital treatment is often followed by weak aftercare systems**, which matters for both management and prevention of recurrence [N7-R1][N7-R3].

### 3. Context and limitations of available data

The available evidence is **important but incomplete**. The strongest direct source is the **Philippines national suicide review**, which uses **Philippine Health Statistics** [N1-F1]. However, the review also notes that **suicide is a low priority in many Western Pacific countries due to competing health problems, stigma, and poor understanding of its incidence and aetiology** [N1-F1]. This implies that **data may be underreported or underestimated** in practice.

A major reliability concern is **stigma and misclassification**. The evidence reports that **suicide is likely under-reported because of its non-acceptance by the Catholic Church and the associated disgrace and stigma to the family**, and that **suicide deaths are likely misclassified as injury of undetermined intent or accidents** [N1-F1]. This is important because **stigma can distort reporting and classification**, especially for suicide and self-harm [N1-F1].

The methodological evidence is **mixed in source type**. The available studies include **reviews, qualitative studies, school surveys, and policy reports**, so **direct hospital-record studies are limited** [N1-R1][N2-F2][N5-F3]. The WHO investment case report adds important context by emphasizing **mental health services governance and access**, and by stating that **enhancing the quality of existing surveillance systems and establishing new systems is essential** for suicide prevention in the region [N5-F3]. This implies that the data may be **fragmented across different systems** and that **surveillance quality varies** [N5-F3].

Common exclusions and underreporting issues include:

- **Stigma-related underreporting**
- **Misclassification of suicide deaths**
- **Under-reporting in sensitive cases**
- **School-based surveys missing non-school-going adolescents and vulnerable groups**
- **Facility-level records and post-pandemic surveys introducing bias** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3]
